note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

constraints: 0 <= a, b < n and a != b; repeated connections allowed
clarifyingQuestions: What exactly is returned: the count of pairs or the pairs themselves?
Are pairs ordered or unordered?
Can a connection repeat?
hints: Friend groups are connected components.
Counting pairs inside groups is easier than counting pairs across groups.
Subtract the within-group pairs s(s-1)/2 from all n(n-1)/2 pairs, with group sizes from a union-find.
invariants: each union merges two groups and adds their sizes
the total number of pairs is fixed at n(n-1)/2
tradeoffs: Union-find avoids building adjacency lists; BFS is equally fast but uses more memory
hack2hire:692d2a491abcca80b11223bf.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: count pairs in different friend groups

clarifyingQuestions: Is the result a string or a list of strings?
Can an obstacle be placed twice at the same position?
Can the checked range reach below position 0?
hints: A check asks whether any placed obstacle lies in [x - size, x - 1].
All positions that will ever be placed are known in advance, so they can be compressed.
Keep a Fenwick tree of placed positions over the compressed order and count the obstacles inside each checked range with two binary searches.
invariants: each position is counted at most once
a check sees exactly the placements that come before it
chooseWhen: Online range-occupancy queries where all keys are known in advance
tradeoffs: An ordered set gives the same bound online; the offline Fenwick tree needs only arrays
hack2hire:6a1e2e688b879849ebc1089e.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: place obstacles and check free blocks

clarifyingQuestions: What are the class and method names?
What is returned when no user has logged in exactly once?
Can a user who logged in twice ever become a one-time visitor again?
hints: Once a user logs in a second time they can never again be a one-time visitor.
Users who logged in exactly once are ordered by their first login, like a queue.
Keep a count per user and a queue of first logins; on a query, drop heads whose count is above 1 (each user is dropped at most once).
invariants: queue entries before the head are never answers again
every user appears in the queue at most once
chooseWhen: Streams that ask for the first element with a property that, once lost, never returns
tradeoffs: Lazy deletion keeps login O(1); an ordered dict also works with eager deletion
hack2hire:688aefae3867670cfb894129.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: first user with exactly one login

constraints: -1e9 <= stockPrice[i] <= 1e9 (negative values allowed by the author for generality)
clarifyingQuestions: What is optimised: the sum, the length or something else?
Is the inequality stockPrice[j] + j >= stockPrice[i] + i as written?
Must the subsequence be non-empty?
hints: The condition only compares key = price + index of consecutive picks.
Balanced subsequences are exactly those whose keys never decrease.
dp[j] adds price[j] to the best non-negative dp among earlier keys <= key[j]; a prefix-maximum Fenwick tree over compressed keys answers that.
invariants: the Fenwick tree holds the best dp of every processed index at its key
a negative best prefix is replaced by 0 (start fresh)
tradeoffs: O(n^2) DP is simpler but too slow at 1e5
hack2hire:6a513eaa665efda9311f609d.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: maximum balanced subsequence sum

clarifyingQuestions: Is the answer the team size or the team members?
Is a one-person team always valid?
Are the bounds inclusive?
hints: Removing a member never raises the counts of anyone else, so feasibility is monotone in the team size.
For a fixed size k, scan developers from lowest skill: the j-th pick has j lower and k - 1 - j higher teammates.
Binary search k and greedily take every developer whose limits allow the current position in the team.
invariants: taken-so-far equals the lower-teammate count of the next pick
feasibility of size k implies feasibility of k - 1
chooseWhen: Maximising a size when feasibility of a size is monotone and checkable greedily
tradeoffs: The greedy check is O(n), so binary search adds only a log factor
hack2hire:6a95d744cddc54478ddf6a6d.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: largest team meeting skill limits

clarifyingQuestions: Is the output the shelf per book or the final shelf counts?
Is limit[i] at least 1 and at most numShelves?
Are ties broken by the smallest index?
hints: Simulate a few books: counts never increase from left to right.
With non-increasing counts the minimum over a prefix is its last shelf, and the tie rule picks the first shelf with that count.
Track the first index of each count value; placing a book moves that index one to the right.
invariants: count[0] >= count[1] >= ... >= count[numShelves - 1]
first[v] is the smallest shelf holding exactly v books
chooseWhen: Simulations whose state keeps a monotone shape
tradeoffs: A segment tree needs no structural insight but costs O(log n) per book
hack2hire:677de8b2052a260e0165706a.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: shelf chosen for each book

constraints: every element is one printable ASCII character
clarifyingQuestions: Is the comparison case-sensitive?
Is an empty filtered sequence a palindrome?
May ignoreArray contain duplicates?
hints: Filtering into a new array costs O(n) extra space, which the preview discourages.
Two pointers can skip ignored characters in place.
Put ignoreArray in a set; move left and right inward past ignored characters and compare.
invariants: characters outside [left, right] already matched in pairs
ignored characters are never compared
chooseWhen: Palindrome checks with filtering under tight memory
tradeoffs: The set costs O(k) space, small because ignoreArray is short
hack2hire:68ace5011bf7d2097f647f50.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: palindrome after skipping ignored characters

constraints: pop and peek only on non-empty versions
clarifyingQuestions: How are versions represented: returned stack objects or handles?
Does pop create a new version or return an existing one?
What do pop and peek do on an empty stack?
hints: Copying a stack per version costs O(n) per operation.
A singly linked list can share its tail: pushing onto any node creates one new node.
Name each version by its top node; push appends (parent, value, size + 1) to arrays and pop returns the parent.
invariants: size[v] = size[parent[v]] + 1 for v > 0
existing nodes are never modified
tradeoffs: Integer handles keep the trace JSON-friendly; returning stack objects would be closer to a native API
hack2hire:677f4db36fee41e51af73dd6.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: versioned stack with integer handles

constraints: 1 <= board length; total pins over all boards <= 2e5
1 <= pin <= 1e9; pins within a board are distinct
clarifyingQuestions: Can pin1 equal pin2?
What if a pin is on no board?
Is relatedness transitive across several boards?
hints: Pins and boards form a graph; relatedness is connectivity.
All pins on one board are connected, so linking each to the board's first pin suffices.
Use a union-find keyed by pin value and compare the roots of pin1 and pin2.
invariants: pins on one board share a root after it is processed
roots only change by union
chooseWhen: Connectivity queries over groups of items
tradeoffs: BFS over a pin-board graph also works but builds adjacency lists
hack2hire:6827b84d285cf34924f48286.variantLabel: Inferred variant 1: are two pins related

constraints: 1 <= board length; total pins over all boards <= 2e5
1 <= pin <= 1e9; pins within a board are distinct
clarifyingQuestions: Is the distance counted in boards or in pins?
What is returned when the pins are not related?
Is the answer 1 when one board holds both pins?
hints: Boards are the steps of the route; pins are the junctions.
Breadth-first search over a bipartite pin-board graph finds the fewest boards.
Index boards by pin, start from every board holding pin1 at distance 1, and expand each board and each pin once.
invariants: boards are dequeued in non-decreasing distance
each board and each pin is expanded at most once
tradeoffs: The bipartite BFS avoids building board-to-board edges, which can be quadratic
hack2hire:6913ed33fa8a311e42671e5d.variantLabel: Inferred variant 2: fewest boards between two pins

constraints: values are distinct members of A, 2..10, J, Q, K
clarifyingQuestions: Can the straight wrap around (Q, K, A, 2, 3)?
Are the inputs always distinct?
Is "10" given as "10" or "T"?
hints: Five distinct values are consecutive exactly when max - min == 4.
Only the ace has two possible ranks.
Check max - min == 4 once with the ace low and once with it high.
invariants: ranks are distinct
the ace takes a single rank per check
chooseWhen: Consecutive-run checks over small distinct sets
tradeoffs: Sorting is unnecessary because distinctness makes the range test exact

constraints: ids match [A-Za-z0-9]{1,10}; names match [A-Z][a-z]{0,11} optionally followed by a space and a second such word
total output length <= 4e6 characters (bounds the depth)
clarifyingQuestions: In what order should siblings appear?
Is there a trailing newline?
Can the input contain cycles or several CEOs?
hints: The chart is a pre-order walk of the management tree.
Group the reports of each manager first, keeping their input order.
Walk iteratively with a stack, pushing reports in reverse so the first report is printed first, and join the lines once.
invariants: a manager is printed before all of its reports
the dash count is four times the depth
chooseWhen: Printing trees given as parent links
tradeoffs: An explicit stack avoids recursion limits on deep charts
hack2hire:691e0f0208ad7861624b5677.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: indented org chart text

constraints: 1 <= race length; total entries over all races <= 2e5
names match [A-Za-z]{1,12}; names within one race are distinct
clarifyingQuestions: How are ties on points broken?
Do riders outside the top 3 count as participants?
Can a race be empty?
hints: Only the first three places earn points.
A hash map from name to total accumulates the season.
Scan the map once, keeping the higher total, or the smaller name on equal totals.
invariants: each race adds at most 30 points in total
the running best is the maximum (total, -name) seen so far

tradeoffs: Sorting all riders is O(r log r); a single scan suffices for the winner

constraints: 1 <= race length; total entries over all races <= 2e5
names match [A-Za-z]{1,12}; names within one race are distinct
clarifyingQuestions: Is the output the winner or the full standings?
What breaks ties: wins, countback or name?
Are riders with 0 points listed?

Collect points and the counts of 1st, 2nd and 3rd places in one pass.
Sort once with the composite key (-points, -firsts, -seconds, -thirds, name).

constraints: each pref[i] is a permutation of 0..m-1
clarifyingQuestions: Is the ranking by first-place votes with later positions as tie-breaks?
How are songs tied at every position ordered?
Do all users rank all songs?
hints: Count, for every song, how many users put it at each position.
Comparing two songs means comparing their count rows lexicographically, larger first.
Sort the ids by the negated count row, then by id.

each position column sums to n

constraints: vehicle ids match [A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,10} and are not "server"
chunk ids match [a-z0-9]{1,8}; 1 <= chunks per event; total chunk ids <= 2e5
clarifyingQuestions: How is contribution measured: chunks sent, distinct chunks, or downstream reach?
Are vehicles that only received data ranked?
How are ties ordered?
hints: The server is the origin, not a vehicle, so it is never ranked.
Split each chunk list and add its length to the sender.
Register every receiver with 0, then sort by (-contribution, id).

contributions only grow

clarifyingQuestions: Is any valid arrangement accepted, or a specific one?
What is returned when no arrangement exists?
May neighborhood sizes change?
hints: A number with c copies must go to c different neighborhoods.
Placing the numbers with the most copies first never hurts (an exchange argument, as in the Gale-Ryser construction).
Use a max-heap of (copies, number): each neighborhood pops its size many entries and pushes back the ones with copies left.
invariants: no number is taken twice for the same neighborhood
remaining copies always sum to the remaining capacity
chooseWhen: Distributing repeated items into groups without repeats inside a group
tradeoffs: The canonical tie rule makes the output checkable exactly but is an author choice
hack2hire:67eae60e4c9bb801bfd0ef48.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: canonical rearrangement or []

clarifyingQuestions: What happens after N is made even: halving, division by m, or something else?
What is returned: the array, its sum, or the sum modulo m?
Which copy of a repeated maximum is chosen?
hints: Only the current maximum changes, so the order of equal maxima does not matter for the final multiset.
A max-heap gives the maximum in O(log n).
Pop the maximum, push (N - N % 2) / 2, repeat k times (stop once it is 0), then sum and reduce modulo m.
invariants: the multiset changes in one element per operation
values never increase
tradeoffs: Stopping at a zero maximum skips useless operations when k is large
hack2hire:688fb256b3f942cc1004c00e.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: halve the maximum k times, sum modulo m
